title: Webmaster a Manifesto for Everyone
description: I'm reclaiming the title of 'webmaster' as the multidisciplinary creator who designs, develops, writes, and advocates for their own corner of the web and will save the world. Tracing the history from 1993 to the present, I argue that anyone can become a webmaster with minimal tools. Webmastery is an act of digital repatriation and human agency against corporate platforms and AI orchestration.
fullText:
A week ago, when I was working on my project for HTML Day 2026 I stumbled upon this passage from an essay on blink and marquee tags:

At the time, there was a new breed of web professionals proudly labeled “webmasters.” Part designer, part developer and part evangelist, webmasters held enough esoteric knowledge about the web to manage, edit and create websites, both large and small.

— Jay Hoffman (August 28th, 2017)

And that's when everything clicked for me.

Over the past year, I've written dozens of articles on the Independent Web. Forty-two essays on principles, technical tutorials, accessibility, and advocacy.

And, in a way, it has all been leading to this manifesto. Only through months of research and getting to know many kind and talented people and building things myself have I finally understood the true power of the webmaster.

I think this will be the most important thing I'll ever write, and I wish to share it with you. With everyone.

The earliest webmasters were unauthorized, self-taught, one-person operations. The first webmaster was a woman, Stanford librarian Louise Addis.

It was a few years after Tim Berners-Lee christened the first web server at CERN at the end of 1990, and published the first website info.cern.ch on August 6th, 1991[1].

The webmaster was first understood as the Internet's equivalent to the real-world postmaster.

"Other protocols have defacto standards for well known mailbox names, such as USENET@domain for NNTP (see [RFC977]), and WEBMASTER@domain for HTTP (see [HTTP])."

— RFC 2142, "Mailbox Names for Common Services, Roles and Functions," Dave Crocker, Internet Mail Consortium. (May 1997)

This RFC—alongside <POSTMASTER@domain> (required by RFC 822)—is what cemented "webmaster" as the canonical, protocol-level point-of-contact role for a website.

"The word “webmaster” comes from a similar role defined in the original specification for email called the postmaster, which in turn comes from the similarly named government position Postmaster General. You can think of the postmaster as an email administrator. The idea being that you can email postmater[sic] @ some domain, and always be connected directly to somebody that could fix a problem with the email. That remains a reserved name today on any email inbox. The webmaster served a pretty similar purpose on the web."

— Jay Hoffman, "What Happened to the Webmaster" (June 16, 2020)

And thus, webmaster@domain was already the de facto email inbox address tied to the HTTP protocol itself.

The label and title quickly grew into something far more than that, though.

"At first it referred to that frustrated techie who set up the rogue Web server without company authorization, coded HTML by hand in a text editor, FTP'd the files to the server, and in his spare time answered all the incoming corporate e-mails, usually also without company authorization."

— Brian Wold, "What Happened to the Webmaster? (And other misleading titles)" (May 12, 2006)

The era that conjures "webmaster" most strongly began in the mid 90's, as Beverly Hills Internet was launched, now known as GeoCities.

"[T]he point about the web before social networks or before Web 2.0 is not that you had a profile on GeoCities, but that you had a chance to build your cyber home outside of it, you could exist and grow outside of a centralized service."

— Olia Lialina, quoted in Cybercultural by Richard MacManus (March 7, 2025)

A culture developed as people realized anybody could make their own website. 88x31 buttons, blinkies, .GIFs, web rings, visitor counters, guestbooks. All originate from this time.

"In 1996, the web was littered with black-and-yellow-striped animated .gifs reveling in metaphors of road construction... 'This site under construction' was the default home page disclaimer, until everyone realized that the inherent nature of the web was that it would be perpetually under construction."

— Fresher Styles for Web Designers, O'Reilly (December 2008)

While GeoCities is fondly remembered now, it certainly had its problems and issues. Similarly, there were other platforms at the time as well, such as Tripod, Angelfire, and Homestead. It can be easy to revise history into an idealized monoculture.

"It was not a paradise for early web makers. It was not even a good web hosting service. It was free and not worse than others, that's why webmasters endured the pain of clumsy page builders, interventions from commercial scripts being injected into their pages, accidental file deletions, etc…"

— "GeoCities' Afterlife and Web History," by Olia Lialin, One Terabyte of Kilobyte Age (July 30, 2019)

Over 38 million pages were deleted when Yahoo shut down the platform in 2009.

As sites grew and the Internet evolved from the expectation of a handful of HTML files located in /var/www/html/ into instead a complex beast of software and content management systems, the "one person does everything" model stopped being the default, and the title became a culture-war topic among web professionals.

Schisms grew from the complexity. The Internet became a vector for business, and then the way to make money as the dotcom bubble inflated. People needed to specialize, whether that was to design for the front-end, or program and administrate the server from the back-end. You needed usability specialists and network engineers and search engine optimizers.

Dammit Jim, I’m a Webmaster, not a Digital Government Web Content Communications and Application Development Knowledge Management Specialist! ...or am I?

Is the term webmaster an accurate description of the responsibilities of today’s web professional, or is that moniker just a quaint artifact from the simpler, earliest days of the web where someone akin to a similarly quaint notion of a Ringmaster juggled a circus of unwieldy text, spinning logos and blinking text?

— David Kitzmiller, FCC Webmaster, Mastering the Web: An Old-Fashioned Notion? (August 12, 2010)

Perhaps the clearest and most citable marker of the term's formal retirement from mainstream professional use is when Google rebranded "Google Webmasters" to "Google Search Central" in 2020. An institutional funeral.

"Merriam-Webster claims the first known use of the word 'webmaster' was in 1993, years before Google even existed. However, the term is becoming archaic, and according to the data found in books, its use is in sharp decline. A user experience study we ran revealed that very few web professionals identify themselves as webmasters anymore. They're more likely to call themselves Search Engine Optimizer (SEO), online marketer, blogger, web developer, or site owner, but very few 'webmasters.' In brainstorming our new name, we realized that there's not one term that perfectly summarizes the work people do on websites."

— Google Search Central Blog (Nov 12, 2020)

It is your innate human right to create.

All of the above was pretext for this: You can be a webmaster right now. You can create a website right now. Yes, you. Your website can look however you want it to, and function in any way you want. It can have whatever you want on it.

You can look up tutorials, and you can have your questions answered by humans just by joining forums, IRC channels, and independent platforms. The act of creating and learning inherently places you in the community.

Generally speaking, we have been deceived into thinking many broad falsehoods:

When plainly laid out like this, it's easy to see how we've been conned into a cynical, pessimistic—even misanthropic view of things. Companies worth billions of dollars have a bottom line that depends on the general population to continue believing all of the above.

Our perspective on technology and other people has been greatly distorted into the negative. In reality, the Internet has terabytes of high-quality resources to learn from. There are thousands of people just like you looking for connection, hungry for a better vision of the future, wanting to cultivate nourishing hobbies. You are so capable.

The idea that one person cannot master all aspects of the web, as the webmaster was once known to, is demonstrably false.

Be optimistic about your capabilities and the willingness of others to help you. Be skeptical of anybody who attempts to divide or gatekeep, proclaiming the mandated use or superiority of a specific tool or platform.

Likewise, I want to note that searching for "return of the webmaster" in 2026 may lead you to discussions of the "agentic web" or "orchestration," a euphemism for somebody who employs generative AI to do the multidisciplinary work that comes with being a webmaster. Those who manage a stack of expensive large language models, those who are prompt engineers for static site generators, and those who neglect to take the time to learn for themselves, unwilling to put in the effort themselves (or thinking they're incapable to).

That's not what this is. My manifesto is not about becoming an orchestrator. Being a webmaster means becoming a sovereign creator. We are not reclaiming the title of "webmaster" only to then offload the work and art onto chatbots. We are reclaiming it because it is the only title that remains which still carries the weight of total, unapologetic human agency over our digital lives.

To be a Webmaster, you need a computer, a text editor, and a way to host. That's it.

You don't need a degree in computer science. You don't need a $50/month subscription to a proprietary builder. You don't even need the money to buy a domain name if you don't have the cash.

If you don't have a computer or Internet yourself, you could be sitting in a public library on a recycled Chromium machine and still you have everything you need to become a Webmaster. There are not gatekeepers at the doors of the World Wide Web. Like many other things in life, the only lock is the one we put on our own ambitions.

A Webmaster is not just a developer. You are a UX/UI designer, you are a writer and editor, you are an accessibility specialist, and an advocate for others to reclaim their digital autonomy. You are a creator, rather than a consumer. And you are capable of all these things.

You will wrestle with semantic markup to make a page accessible. You will agonize over typeface kerning and colour palettes. You will write prose and publish your weird obsessions and link to your Internet neighbours. You will manage server logs, tweak the .htaccess file, and you will decide and design the architecture of your digital home.

This is not a career path, this is a craft. This is the last best multidisciplinary sandbox, both creative and technical, all rendered on an index.html.

And there is no wrong answer. Serve your website over the Gemini protocol. SSH into the Tildeverse and build a terminal-based homepage alongside strangers. Set up a homelab in your closet using the old, defunct family computer. There are a million ways to do this. The only wrong answer is sitting on the sidelines believing you don't belong in the arena with us.

Corporate social media platforms we used to call the "new public square" have been astroturf'd, bulldozed, and sold to the highest-bidding fascist oligarch. Your existence is a rental, your voice is a throttled lottery. Your so-called "community" is at the mercy of a billionaire's whim.

Building your own website is an act of digital repatriation.

Creating your own corner of the Internet reclaims one of the only mediums where we retain freedom, creativity, and autonomy.

With the plethora of hosting options available, you can migrate if terms of service change to your disliking. There's no pay-to-play visibility. There's just you, text, and the open protocols of the web.

The most effective way the power structures of our age have oppressed us is by making us feel as though we are stupid, as though we are incapable of learning.

Many of us have been convinced coding is arcane magic, that servers are eldritch horrors, and that computer science is reserved for child prodigies and those who are privileged to just "naturally get it."

A user who is afraid of the machine and doubts their own capabilities is one that will surrender and pay for a solution.

You are not incapable. There is a lot to learn, yes. And the technologies are deep. But do not forget we are still living in the golden age of human knowledge—endless free resources, tutorials, wikis, and forums are available at your fingertips.

I will repeat myself and say the only barrier that exists is the one you construct in your mind.

You require grit, determination, and a "why." This is your why. The desire to express yourself. The hunger to build something truly of your own. The need to connect with other humans.

Let me be clear: this is not about "IndieWeb" specs, it isn't about the "Small Web" or "SmolWeb." It isn't a retro-revival nostalgia trip, pining for GeoCities and AOL dial-up tones.

Those are all labels, clubs, and memberships. Standards with elitism and in-group and cliques and gatekeeping as a result.

What I'm talking about is universal. It's not about specific mechanics, it's about a philosophy. It is a big tent.

It doesn't matter if you speak English. It doesn't matter if you don't know how to spell words right in your native tongue. It doesn't matter if you don't know a single line of JavaScript, either.

And it certainly doesn't matter if you think you have "nothing interesting to say." I promise you do. All humans have value, we have our hobbies, our frustrations, our obsessions and small thoughts. Putting this in writing on a page you build with your own hands means you're contributing to a richer, stranger, more wonderful ecosystem.

I stand on the shoulders of giants. I am not the first to write a web manifesto, nor the last. I myself am nobody special, nor anybody with authority. I am mere conduit for a message that desperately needs to be heard.

I give credit to Tantek Çelik, Amber Case, Aaron Parecki, Crystal Beasley, and Kevin Marks for founding IndieWebCamp in Portland, Oregon in 2011.

I give credit to Daniel Murray's melonking.net as a foundational "web revival" artifact.

"[The web revival] is a riff on the 20th century American folk music revival, and it implies that early personal sites, like those hosted on GeoCities, were culturally significant as digital folk art."

— Daniel Murray (Melonking), quoted in New_ Public (September 7, 2025)

I give credit to webmistress Sadness, who has been sharing resources on web mastery for years, and was the founder of the now defunct Yesterweb, served as many people's first experience of the indie-web-crafting scene.

"In the earlier iterations of this manifesto, I made the mistake of focusing too heavily on the creation of personal websites as the main method of fighting against the exploitative capitalist hellscape that has become our Internet... For example, we can work on transforming social relations online."

— Sadness, Internet manifesto (May 2023)

I give credit to James G., who has been blogging about the independent Internet for over six years, who hosts the podcast Wonders of Webweaving, and who has recently founded the Web Writers' Collective, which is open to anyone.

I give credit to Alexandra and Kaylee for the community and resources of 32-bit Café. I give credit to Adam Newbold for the community and services of omg.lol.

There are hundreds of people who have dedicated thousands of hours in trying to make the web more human and joyous for all.

We can create a more human web right now. The world is in dire straits, and I'm reminded of the words of Carl Sagan, coincidentally written at the dawn of the webmaster:

“In our obscurity, in all this vastness, there is no hint that help will come from elsewhere to save us from ourselves.”

— Carl Sagan, Pale Blue Dot (1994)

There are those who see the act of webmastery as "only" a hobby and pastime—and I say this is not mutually exclusive to world-saving. The personal is political. Our ability to maintain our joy and ourselves is, itself, resistance.

Here is another falsehood I want to emphasize: Our right to freely express ourselves is never a guarantee. The past thirty years of the Internet have been an explosive, chaotic experiment in the commons and the human condition. But the freedom of expression we've been granted is not a given or perpetual promise, and it is extremely foolish to think we will have this for the next ten years, let alone forever.

Start as you are, with what you have, while you still have time to do so.

Exercise your innate human right to create.

Be a developer. Be a designer. Be a writer. Be a systems administrator. Be a philosopher. Be a Webmaster.

It is the most punk rock, anti-establishment, liberating thing you can do in the 21st century. And yeah, it is fucking awesome.

Over the past year I've written forty-two essays on this subject. Here are the ones I think are most worth a beginner's time.

You will find claims that "webmaster" originated from CERN itself across SEO and marketing blogs, but this is mere folk etymology I couldn't independently verify. Multiple independent lexicographic sources mark 1993 as the first attested year of the webmaster, such as the OED and Etymonline. ↩︎

fullText:
Australia’s corporate watchdog says PM is the figure most commonly used in deepfakes to promote phony investment opportunities

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

There has been a steep rise in scammers luring victims into phony investment opportunities using deepfakes of celebrities and politicians, Australia’s corporate watchdog has warned.

And Anthony Albanese is the figure most commonly co-opted.

Real footage of the prime minister, overlaid with fake audio promising Australians can invest $4,000 to earn $40,000 a month, appears in one video online.

“This is not just another scam product,” the deepfake Albanese says, falsely describing it as an “official platform” with a government guarantee.

The Australian Securities and Investment Commission (Asic) dealt with more than 19,400 scams last financial year, almost triple the amount in the year before.

Artificial intelligence is making it increasingly easy to generate deepfakes, it warned.

Fake celebrities were just the beginning. Scammers have built networks of fake brands, websites, reviews, news articles and videos that work together to convince victims to ultimately give them money, which ends up going to overseas criminals, Asic said.

According to reports to the National Anti-Scam Centre’s Scamwatch, Australians lost $7.4m to the top 10 impersonated public figures, and Albanese was at the top of the list.

In one video, a deepfake of the prime minister promises people can earn $35 an hour, which is “about $850 per day” and “over $25,000 per month”, according to the Australian Financial Review. The disinformation and dodgy maths are presented with an American accent.

“Greetings. From the first day I became prime minister, I wanted to improve the tax system. We will not fully get rid of taxes, of course, but any resident will be able to receive dividends from them,” the fake says.

Economists Tom Piotrowski and Stephen Koukoulas; ABC financial journalist Alan Kohler; and politicians Jacqui Lambie and Angus Taylor (showing Lambie confronting Taylor on Insiders about patronising people) make up the top five.

They were followed by entrepreneur Dick Smith, billionaire Gina Rinehart, economist Alan Oster, Pauline Hanson and the late radio legend John Laws.

“It is important to note that scammers are receptive to broader changes in the news cycle and will opportunistically change which celebrities they impersonate to capitalise on topical issues,” Asic warned.

Last financial year, Asic took down 5,476 phishing scam hyperlinks, almost four times as many as the previous year; 7,051 fake investment platforms, 2.5 times higher; and 3,106 cryptocurrency scams, an increase of almost 30%.

“The presence of polished content, familiar branding or convincing testimonials does not mean an investment is legitimate,” the Asic chair, Sarah Court, said.

“AI is making investment scams more convincing and harder to detect. A simple online search is not enough to verify whether an opportunity is legitimate.

“Before investing, consumers should verify website addresses, check whether a person or company is legitimate and who they claim to be, and be wary of urgent calls to act.”

Scamwatch advises consumers to stop before sharing money or information; to check the details independently; and to protect yourself and others by reporting any scams to them, your bank, or cyber.gov.au.

Asic said consumers should check for a certified Australian financial services licence, but also be aware that scammers misuse those licences, so they should check against Asic’s professional registers.

Commonwealth Bank research published earlier this year found about nine in 10 Australians were confident they could spot an AI scam, but in reality they can do so less than half the time.

Deepfakes are also increasingly being used politically. Independent MP Zali Steggall has proposed a bill to crack down on deceptive political advertising, which would require AI-generated content that could mislead voters to be clearly identified.

title: Iran business leader admits U.S. blockade will inflict more economic damage than war, and the ‘worst thing that could happen’ is trying to evade it
description: The head of the Iran-China Joint Chamber of Commerce said "the consequences of the blockade far outweigh those of a direct war."
fullText:
President Donald Trump is doubling down on wielding economic pressure to squeeze Iran as his military options dwindle, and Tehran's business community warned the naval blockade will cause far-reaching harm.

In an interview with Iran's Khabar Online outlet, the head of the Iran-China Joint Chamber of Commerce said "the consequences of the blockade far outweigh those of a direct war."

Majidreza Hariri added that the economic crisis and shortages currently ravaging Iran under the blockade are more severe than they were during the 40-day war earlier this year.

As a result, Iran must find a way to end the blockade one way or another, whether by way of negotiations, pleading, threats or even renewing war against the U.S., he said. That's because trying to cope with the blockade would lead to dangerous spillover effects.

"The worst thing that could happen today is believing that the naval blockade can be circumvented and attempting to govern the country despite its continuation," Hariri said.

He pointed to Iran's decades-long experience under Western sanctions, saying the methods that were used skirt them eventually resulted in a weak economy and rampant corruption.

The U.S. naval blockade also threatens to inflict enormous costs in the short term. For example, transporting a single container between Iran and China via ships costs about $3,000, according to Hariri. But bypassing the blockade by transporting it over land would boost the cost to $12,000.

Given that 2 million containers pass through Iran's southern ports annually, he estimated that heavier trade burdens will translate to about $18 billion in additional transportation costs alone every year.

Relying on land routes to get around the blockade could provide enough necessities to allow for short-term survival, but the economy will eventually "grind to a halt," Hariri predicted.

But he also suggested Iran would retaliate against continued U.S. pressure rather than simply standing by and watching the economy crumble.

"We must also eliminate the perception in the U.S. that it can resort to such an action whenever it wants, and make it understand that the consequences of such a move could be severe," Hariri said.

His warning comes as regime moderates have grown more worried that the U.S. naval blockade that was recently reimposed is bringing Iran's economy close to collapse, sources told the Wall Street Journal.

Iran's deputy foreign minister has also said the economy desperately needs sanctions relief that a deal with the U.S. could provide.

title: Aston Martin’s 2027 Aramco Funding Frozen Amid Middle East Conflict, Insider Reports
description: A major geopolitical crisis is reportedly spilling over into the Formula 1 paddock, threatening to blow a massive hole in Aston Martin’s long-term financial and technical strategy. According to prominent F1 business insider Marc Limacher, Saudi Arabia has frozen its…
fullText:
A major geopolitical crisis is reportedly spilling over into the Formula 1 paddock, threatening to blow a massive hole in Aston Martin's long-term financial and technical strategy.

According to prominent F1 business insider Marc Limacher, Saudi Arabia has frozen its massive title sponsorship with the Silverstone-based team for the 2027 season due to escalating conflicts in the Middle East.

The news broke via a social media post from Limacher, a well-known F1 financial journalist and author of the specialized Business Book GP.

Limacher's post dropped a massive bombshell on the team's financial outlook, claiming that "Saudi Arabia, after several months of discussions, has frozen the sponsorship of the Aston Martin #F1 team for 2027."

The timing of the freeze is especially shocking given the team's previously upward financial trajectory. Aston Martin has been investing heavily in its new AMR Technology Campus, and corporate backing was expected to grow. "Riyadh was supposed to increase its Aramco sponsorship and bring a third sponsor to the team's portfolio," Limacher noted in the post.

The sudden financial reversal appears to be entirely out of executive chairman Lawrence Stroll's control.

According to Limacher, "The war in Iran is delaying the project." With the regional conflict demanding massive economic, defensive, and strategic shifts from the Saudi government, extravagant international marketing expenditures—like global motorsport sponsorships—appear to be taking an immediate back seat.

If Aramco's funding is indeed frozen for 2027, it could spell disaster for Aston Martin's most critical transition.

In late 2023, Aramco signed a highly publicized contract extension to remain the exclusive title sponsor of the team through the 2028 season. However, Aramco's involvement isn't merely financial; it is a foundational pillar of the team's on-track performance.

Starting in 2026, Aston Martin became the official works team for Honda power units. As part of that strategic alliance, Aramco was specifically tasked with developing the 100% sustainable advanced fuels and specialized lubricants required under the FIA's new 2026 engine regulations.

If Saudi Arabia pulls its financial and technical support from the project just one year into the new Honda partnership, Aston Martin could find itself scrambling for both a title sponsor and a cutting-edge fuel supplier right in the middle of a championship window.

Neither Aston Martin nor Aramco has issued an official statement regarding the reported freeze, but the paddock will undoubtedly be watching the Middle East closely as the situation develops.

fullText:
An independent brewery and hospitality operator has agreed the sale of three of its pubs.

True North Brew Co has given up The British Oak in Mosborough and The Old Grindstone in Crookes, both in Sheffield, along with The Milton Arms in Elsecar, Barnsley.

The company said it wanted to "strengthen and stabilise" its business due to a "challenging period" for the industry.

Owner Kane Yeardley, said: "This has not been an easy decision, but it is a necessary step to secure the long-term future of our company. We are committed to supporting our teams through this transition and ensuring our remaining venues continue to thrive."

The company, which acquired the Abbeydale Picture House in Sheffield in 2025 to transform it into a "premier entertainment venue", said the three pubs had been "an important part of the company's estate".

It said it had relinquished them to secure new ownership that would continue to operate them as pubs, "preserving their character and role" within their local communities.

In 2024, The Waggon and Horses in Sheffield was given a new lease to use a nearby park as its beer garden after True North Brew went into administration in 2023.

Administrators had sold its assets to new owners Cocktails and Craft Beers Ltd and all jobs were saved.

According to Companies House records, in 2023 the new owners successfully applied to change their name to True North Brew Co.

In April, plans were approved for the brewery to convert part of Grade II-listed Walkley Library in Sheffield to include a cafe-bar.

The company said while deciding to sell the three pubs it took a "considered and proactive approach" to protect the long-term health of its wider estate, focusing on "preserving the strength" of the core business.

Is said the sale and transfer was expected to complete within about three months and it remained "fully committed" to supporting the wellbeing and future of its employees.

All affected team members would have the opportunity to transfer to the new owners, it said. For those who wanted to remain with True North Brew Co, every effort would be made to find suitable alternative opportunities within the business.

The company thanked its staff and customers for their "continued support, loyalty, and dedication".

description: Allison Strumeyer says ordering 10,000 pairs of socks before launching doublesoul helped prove demand and gave her the confidence to build the company.
fullText:
Allison Strumeyer wanted experience in finance and a startup before launching her own.

She says working for BlackRock showed her how to work to a high standard.

She launched a sock company that does millions in annual sales.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Allison Strumeyer, cofounder and CEO of doublesoul. It has been edited for length and clarity.

When I was in college at the University of Pennsylvania, I had a side hustle selling T-shirts. I would connect with local artists to feature their work and sell the shirts on campus. I also did pitch competitions with my now-husband, Ben. I've always felt very native to entrepreneurship, and I knew I wanted to start my own business.

Yet, when I graduated, I chose to work at BlackRock. It was intentional: I believed working with a global finance company would give me insights valuable to me as an entrepreneur. BlackRock also taught me how to perform at a high level, in everything from communications to project management.

I was at BlackRock for about two years, then joined Mirror, a startup that was acquired by Lululemon. Mirror was smaller and scrappier, and during my four years there, I learned about scaling a startup. The combination of both experiences left me ready to start my own company.

I always found it interesting that we wear socks more than almost anything else in our wardrobe. But there's little innovation, product development, branding, or design around socks. I felt the category had been ignored, and I believed that we all deserve socks we're excited about.

My husband Ben and I became really emotionally attached to the idea of creating better socks. But we wanted to test the market before diving in. We created a prototype and ordered 10,000 pairs — the minimum order, which was about $100,000 worth of socks.

We shared them with pretty much everyone we'd ever met and asked them to post about the socks. That gave us organic sales and — more importantly — proof of our concept. In 2022, we officially launched Doublesoul.

I chose to stay in my day job as long as possible while we started the company. On social media, people are encouraged to leave their jobs to pursue their own projects, but that felt like dangerous territory to me.

Having that backing gave me the confidence I needed to leave my job. Ben and I knew we would need to sell lots of socks before we could fund a team. But we also wanted to move quickly, so we pursued venture funding. We raised about $2 million.

title: Goat herding hedge: Susquehanna, Kalshi help company offset change in law
description: A goat herding business facing higher wage costs turned to prediction market platform Kalshi to hedge and help offset the possible expense.
fullText:
A goat herding business facing higher payroll costs from a legislative bill turned to prediction market platform Kalshi to hedge and help offset the possible expense.

Tim Arrowsmith, owner of Western Grazers in California, estimates that he pays at least $70,000 per year for each herder when factoring in workers' flight tickets and visa costs. The company, whose goats eat vegetation to help prevent wildfires, has about 4,000 animals and eight herders, who are each paid $60,000 a year.

Arrowsmith was concerned that his annual labor costs could rise to as much as $240,000 per herder after a California wage exemption expired on June 30. This means goat herders must abide by a 2016 assembly bill instead and be paid a set wage for being on-call 24 hours a day, which comes out to about $20,000 a month for each worker. That could cost upwards of $240,000 a year per herder, according to estimates from the California Farm Bureau.

The 2016 bill excludes sheep herders from higher wages, despite stakeholders finding the working conditions for both sheep and goat herders overlap, according to a 2026, state-mandated study from the University of California, Davis.

"The legislature has their study. They have the data. It's simply the lack of will to do the right thing and to make a simple fix," Arrowsmith said.

New-York based startup called Castle learned of Arrowsmith's situation after the company's AI tool was scraping the news to find new businesses to support. Founded by four Stanford graduates, the company is backed by Ribbit Capital and helps businesses of any size to protect itself against financial risks traditional insurances may not cover.

Hedging is a management strategy that helps companies and investment funds offset losses by taking opposing positions in an existing investment. Hedging can include using derivatives like options and futures, along with short selling and inverse ETFs. In this case, a goat herding company hedged on the outcome of California's legislature.

Castle sent out a cold email to Arrowsmith to see if he was interested in structuring a hedge.

"We were fortunate enough to get a response, and then we got on a call with him, and we were really, really moved," said Lucas Cavalieri, co-founder and CEO of Castle. "We really put in the effort to try to provide some sort of coverage for him."

Before Castle reached out, Arrowsmith had no idea what prediction market platform Kalshi was and that a hedge for his business could even exist. That didn't stop Arrowsmith from agreeing to the deal, who is at risk of selling his goats and laying off his herders.

"[Hedging] wasn't something we went looking for," Arrowsmith said. "This is a whole new education for me."

Castle declined to comment on how much it profited from arranging the hedge for Western Grazers.

After Castle identified the risks for Arrowsmith and his company, the startup worked with Susquehanna to make the hedge a reality.

Led by Susquehanna senior trader Eric Passmore, the firm established pricing and the contract terms on Kalshi. Constructing those provisions came after deep research on California's goat herding business, speaking with industry professionals and connecting with Arrowsmith, Passmore said.

The contract has a $500,000 payout that Arrowsmith paid a 10% premium or $50,000 on. That means Arrowsmith receives the payout if California does not "authorizes an alternative wage or provides qualifying relief from goat herder wage and overtime obligations before Oct 1, 2026," according to the Kalshi contract.

The contract can resolve in a multitude of ways with several requirements, including if there is a written order from a state court or federal court on goat herder wages, or if a new law on overtime payment is signed by the governor. Goat herders falling under the same wage criteria as sheep herders is another way for the contract to resolve, according to Kalshi's market rules.

If California does provide regulations that modify goat herder wages by Oct. 1 and align with the contract's conditions, Western Grazers will not receive the six figure payment. This is what Arrowsmith wants.

"The idea that you can trade a specific, minimum wage provision within the California state legislature, it's just something traditional products like wheat futures or corn futures can't handle," Passmore said.

Castle's four founders and Passmore visited Arrowsmith on Aug. 6, after the hedge was fleshed out. The entire process, from reaching out to Arrowsmith to building out the contract, took two and a half weeks, said Castle co-founder and President Bruno Felix Castillo.

Kalshi took a "backseat" in facilitating the hedge, said Nicolas Hull, director of business development at the prediction markets company, who also manages hedging there.

"We went to the markets team, ensured that we had a verifiable data source to pull this from, and we were able to list the market," Hull said.

This isn't the first time the platform's facilitated a hedge. After the Knicks beat the San Antonio Spurs in the first match, a small bar in the Upper East Side ended up covering its customers' tabs since it placed a $5,000 trade on Kalshi that the Knicks would win. The bar won over $13,000 from the Kalshi contract.

For now, Kalshi is more focused on spreading awareness on how hedging works.

"I think for right now, I don't see it being a huge revenue driver short term," Hull said. "Right now, we're focused on building out awareness, getting people to understand how they can use this platform to hedge."

Hedging is still a foreign concept for businesses and traders, but that's likely to change in the coming years, said Castle's co-founder and chief technology officer Arjun Pandey. Like Hull, Pandey added that the public needs exposure on how a hedge on a prediction market works.

"Ten years from now, everyone's gonna know about [hedging]. It's gonna be a whole massive thing. For now, someone has to kickstart that process of educating people," Pandey said.

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

title: Why Japanese firms are being so slow to use AI
description: Japanese risk aversion and conservatism blamed for slow AI take-up by the country's business sector.
fullText:
Facing acute labour shortages, ageing demographics and chronic productivity problems, Japanese companies should be fertile ground for the take-up of artificial intelligence (AI). Yet, compared with the US and UK, adoption in many workplaces remains sluggish and cautious.

Japan's response to AI is beginning to resemble one of the country's slow-moving, traditional Noh plays.

All the masked characters up on stage agree that action is urgent, and the call is repeated with solemn agreement. Yet the actors remain frozen in place.

Great for heightening drama, terrible for addressing the country's immediate difficulties.

Data showing the use of AI in the workplace suggests that Japan has fallen behind. Just 8.4% of Japanese workers use AI as part of their job, according to a report, external at the end of last year by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

US and Japan take action to prop up yen in rare joint move

AI used new levels of 'autonomy and deception' to trick people in safety test

So why is Japan dragging its feet? Austin Xu, co-founder of US start-up Kuse AI, says it is due to Japanese companies being conservative and risk adverse. His business recently set up an office in Japan to sell its AI systems to firms in the country.

"There are organisations where process and consensus culture genuinely slow things down," he says. "Where tolerance for AI mistakes is close to zero, especially in anything client facing. Some would rather leave a role unfilled than let a machine handle it."

Xu says the situation in the US is very different, with some businesses already allowing AI agents far more freedom to boost productivity. "In the US, AI colleagues enter as helpers and gradually become part of the workflow. The attitude [of US bosses] is often - let it try, then correct it."

He adds that Japanese companies need more proof before they trust AI enough to use it.

Parrisa Haghirian, professor of international management at the Kyoto University of Advanced Science, agrees that many Japanese companies are too risk adverse to look at AI.

"The challenges of adopting it are the same as adopting any change in Japanese firms. This is why AI use is still quite limited and cautious, especially in the workplace."

Haghirian also contrasts this with the more entrepreneurial culture of the US, arguing that Japanese firms are highly sensitive to error, uncertainty and reputational risk.

"Since generative AI is still not fully reliable, it is mainly used [in Japan] for low-risk tasks such as writing, summarising, or information gathering, but much less for core operations or decision-making and for improving overall processes," she says.

Japan's healthcare sector is said to be particularly slow to look at AI, with some hospitals yet to even fully digitalise patient files. "Paper documents accumulate at a staggering scale," says one employee at a Japanese hospital, who asked not to be named. "It's like the Stone Age."

The Japanese government is aware of the wider problem of low AI adoption, and is trying to get more companies to take up the technology. Last year its AI Promotion Act was passed, external by the country's parliament.

This aims to use light-touch regulation to encourage businesses to invest 

The government believes that the increased use of AI can help Japan improve its productivity. Currently it continues to have the worst level, external in the G7 group of advanced nations.

Japan's Ministry of Finance says that AI adoption by businesses has already increased substantially,, external with 75% of companies now using the technology, up from 11% five years ago.

However, critics argue that at each of these businesses only a tiny proportion of staff are actually using the AI, and that those who do so are only using it to a very limited extent.

Prof Yasushi Ogasawara, an expert on Japan's social system and technology at Meiji University, says there aren't enough tech-savvy people in the workforce.

"Although the Japanese like playing with gadgets such as smartphones, digital literacy is low here," he says.

This is highlighted by one report earlier this year which said Japan faced a shortfall , externalof almost 800,000 IT professionals by 2030.

Many companies are also said to struggle with out-of-date computer systems, with around 60% more than 20-years-old.

Moreover, Ogasawara adds that Japanese companies are under more pressure to avoid fuelling unemployment than they are to develop AI which could result in job losses.

"The government is talking about AI, re-skilling, digital skills, but in reality, it is difficult to adapt human resources to digital skills because the top priority is to maintain full employment," he says.

But there is a shift in recruitment, with some companies now prioritising "AI literacy" in their new graduate hiring.

In the private sector, larger firms such as Kanematsu, a major general trading company, are hiring savvy graduates such as Uta Yamaguchi who joined in April.

"I use AI quite often at work," she says. "Many of my colleagues use it a lot. For writing emails for my boss, summarising complicated documents, meeting recording and summarising."

But, by contrast with the US, she says AI systems that can autonomously handle multi-step work are still virtually unheard of in Japan.

However, her employer, known for its forward thinking, now has them onboard.

Ogasawara says that "change in Japan is limited". He adds: "Japanese society expects painless reform, so I think it can be said that drastic reform is difficult, to say the least."

Disruption may be a dirty word in Japan, but without it the productivity gains the country needs could remain elusive.

title: Kalshi’s 30-year-old CEO says most business advice is ‘trash’—he doesn’t read management books or listen to podcasts: ‘I’m gonna make it up as I go’
description: Kalshi cofounder Tarek Mansour slams founders for being over-reliant on ‘mostly trash’ business advice—he founded his now-$22 billion prediction market as a college grad.
fullText:
Prediction market Kalshi has exploded in recent years, reaching a $22 billion valuation. For the company's 30-year-old CEO, Tarek Mansour, getting there hasn't meant following the wisdom of business school professors or management gurus—it's been ignoring advice altogether.

"The worst advice that most people get is that you should go and seek out a bunch of advice. There's really no recipe to any of this stuff," Mansour told The New York Times in a recent interview. "People are over-reliant on advice, and people love giving advice because it makes them feel smart and powerful. It's usually mostly trash."

Mansour's skepticism of conventional founder wisdom is backed by his own track record: He and cofounder Luana Lopes Lara have built Kalshi into a platform with four million active users and became self-made billionaires, with estimated net worths of about $2.6 billion each.

And when it comes to his own business approach, Mansour said he's largely learned by doing—opting to even ignore management books or podcasts.

"I have a lot of, I'm gonna make it up as I go," he said on a Sequoia Capitol podcast last month.

"Both of us, we're probably very sort of entrepreneurially illiterate," Mansour said, referring to himself and his cofounder, Lopes Lara. "We haven't read all the books, we haven't watched all the podcasts."

Mansour and Lopes Lara met as classmates at MIT, and with companies like Goldman Sachs, Palantir, Citadel, and Bridgewater Associates on their collective resumes, they were likely headed down lucrative careers in tech and finance.

Instead, less than a year after graduating, they set out to build Kalshi in 2018—initially envisioning the company as a financial exchange where users could buy and sell contracts tied to the outcomes of real-world events. The early years, however, were anything but easy. Kalshi faced regulatory hurdles as it sought approval for its novel business model, and Mansour admitted there were countless times when he wanted to give up.

"Every day you wake up and you're like, 'What am I doing?'" he said.

title: Florida business owners allegedly scattered 1,500 mothballs on beach to send endangered birds packing
description: Two St. Pete Beach business owners allegedly spread 1,500 toxic mothballs on sand to stop black skimmers from nesting and are facing felony charges.
fullText:
Two Florida business owners have been charged with third-degree felonies after allegedly spreading about 1,500 "toxic" mothballs across a beach in hopes of keeping an "imperiled" bird species from nesting there.

If convicted, they could each face up to five years in prison, fines of up to $5,000 and up to five years of probation.

The problem started in late April when beachgoers noticed mothballs on the white, sugary sand on St. Pete Beach in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) and bird-loving volunteers from the Audubon Society mobilized. They plucked about 1,000 of the small, white orbs from the sand behind the Plaza Beach Hotel.

Massachusetts Homeowners Stunned After Town Warns July 4 Flags Threaten Endangered Birds

Then 500 more appeared overnight.

The smelly balls containing pesticides dotted an area where endangered shorebirds known as black skimmers were "attempting to establish a nesting colony," FWC officials said at a news conference. Their placement also meant other wildlife and children "could easily come in contact with them."

It quickly became clear that someone might be targeting the birds, they said.

So FWC investigators flew into action.

The discovery of the mothballs ruffled feathers in the community.

There was "a lot of public outcry," expressing concern for the birds, while investigators tried to locate the source of the mothballs, FWC officials said.

Law enforcement served search warrants, combed through "terabytes" of data and eventually seized cellphones to try to locate the individuals behind the caper.

That work led them to Christopher Monroe, owner and manager of Chris's Beachside Bar, and Robert Czyszczon, owner of the Plaza Beach Hotel, FWC officials said.

Out of fear of lost revenue, the two allegedly hatched a plan to use mothballs to deter birds from congregating on the beach behind their businesses, authorities said.

Hikers Face $25,000 Fine After Off-leash Dog Barked At Grizzly Bear On Banff National Park Trail

Through video surveillance and receipt records, investigators found that Czyszczon spent about $60 buying "a large quantity" of mothballs at a Walmart the day before they first appeared on the beach, FWC officials said.

Upon examining his phone, investigators found "incriminating" text messages between him and fellow business owner Monroe discussing their objections to the native fowl.

Text conversations revealed plans for placement of the mothballs on the beach, officials said. That's what led investigators to Monroe as a suspect.

The men discussed how they "were going to do something" to prevent the birds from nesting on the beach, FWC officials said.

Black skimmers don't nest in trees. They kick beach sand to make depressions on the ground. Then they lay their eggs and raise their young near the surf.

"They're the worst birds," one of the men allegedly wrote in anticipation of nesting season.

"The bird people will put up fence around the area, and then the beach people will not be able to get to and from because they will fence around that space."

Cellphone tower data showed Monroe's phone was at the same location as Czyszczon's phone on both nights when the mothballs appeared on the beach, FWC officials said.

The men feared that nests on the beach would lead to fewer customers and less money being spent there, authorities said.

"Why didn't you tell me we lose $25,000 to $50,000?" one allegedly wrote in a text.

Monroe and Czyszczon were charged with illegal dumping, a third-degree felony, according to Pinellas County court records. They also were charged with the "attempted take of a state-listed imperiled species by harassment," a misdemeanor, according to FWC officials.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

About 6,800 black skimmers live in Florida. FWC officials estimate that several hundred live on the beaches of Pinellas County.

The pesticide in mothballs can harm people and wildlife that come into contact with their vapors, according to an educational publication by the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (IFAS).

"With any pesticide, the label is the law," Brett W. Bultemeier, director of the UF/IFAS Pesticide Information Office, wrote in a 2021 educational publication about mothballs. "The label language is not simply a set of directions. Rather, they are requirements that are legally enforceable."

The birds probably weren't hurt by the "harassment," FWC officials said.

But it did delay their nesting, they said. That pushes the date that their young can fledge from the nest further back in the season. And that could put them in danger.

A big storm at the end of hurricane season, which ends on Nov. 30, "can wipe out a colony if those young birds haven't fledged yet," an FWC official said.

An attorney for Czyszczon did not respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital. Court records indicate that Monroe doesn't have an attorney. He couldn't be reached for comment.

title: Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino appears to be trying to return to business as usual after the failed World Cup private investment plan - but it may not be that easy.
fullText:
Gianni Infantino stepped off a plane in Cali and was greeted on the runway by the president of the Colombian Football Federation.

Ramon Jesurun, a close ally of Infantino's, saw it as a chance to show his support, with the two men smiling in a photo opportunity for the federation's Instagram account.

Infantino had not travelled to Colombia for any run-of-the-mill meeting on Friday. He would attend the inauguration of the country's new president Abelardo de la Espriella.

Infantino was accompanied by Alejandro Dominguez, the president of South America's football governing body Conmebol, who praised both his record and the "enormously successful" 2026 World Cup, saying "we stand with Gianni".

This is the life of a Fifa president.

It involves building ties with some of the most powerful people in the world, shown by Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump.

Before the biggest scandal to hit his tenure - the aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise plan - Infantino was an incredibly powerful figure who appeared bulletproof.

Now, after an apology and stated desire to withstand the backlash of his plan to sell a stake in the men's World Cup to private equity firms, Infantino appears to be trying to return to business as usual.

Uefa's threat to boycott Fifa tournaments still stands. That will be tested with the Fifa Under-20 World Cup set to kick off in Poland in 29 days.

Perhaps emboldened by the support he has received from outside Europe in recent days, Infantino is not going to stand down easily.

But what exactly is the role of the Fifa president?

A cavalcade of blacked out Mercedes, flanked by police cars, rolled into the Fifa headquarters in Rabat, Morocco, earlier this week.

Infantino had summoned a select few members of the Fifa management board to discuss his plan to sell off 21% of the commercial and ticketing business to a private equity firm.

This is how the Swiss-Italian travels - in between flights on the Qatar Airways Executive jet which has been made available to him. The plane enabled him to take up to three flights a day, watching two games, throughout the 2026 World Cup.

That type of arrival does look presidential - only more like a president of a country than a sports body.

It enables him to travel the globe, visiting Fifa's official offices like Rabat, where he was based over the past week as the Fifa Forward Enterprise controversy developed.

In his role Infantino is expected to visit the 211 member nations, to see the grassroots projects Fifa has funded.

Part of his remit is to unify football, which cannot be achieved from within the Fifa headquarters in Zurich.

It requires international travel to attend confederation meetings, and the global tournaments Fifa organises. Infantino needs to build relationships with officials and politicians.

In April, before the Fifa Congress in Vancouver, local authorities rejected a request for a level-four motorcade, usually reserved for heads of state or the Pope.

New Zealand police said they had declined a similar request during the 2023 Women's World Cup.

Alongside the cavalcade of cars and the private charter flights comes a large salary, too, three times what he first earned when elected in 2016.

Infantino, who was paid about £1.3m 10 years ago, now takes home about £4m - a base salary of £2.2m plus a confirmed variable bonus payment of £1.8m.

His predecessor Sepp Blatter was paid a £2.6m package for his final year as Fifa president.

Infantino gets a 'per diem' too to cover expenses and living costs, worth £20,500 a year on top of his salary.

As the head of the most popular sport in the world, it should be expected that there is a wage to match.

Infantino would argue that by driving record revenues and funding for member associations, he has proven he is worth the salary.

Infantino's alliance with Trump seemed to have elevated his status even further.

Many in world football felt that this began to come at the expense of his responsibilities in football.

In May 2025, Infantino had been on a diplomatic tour of the Middle East with Trump and turned up two hours late for the Fifa Congress in Paraguay.

Uefa accused Infantino of prioritising "private political interests" and staged a walk-out.

There was also the Fifa Peace Prize, awarded to Trump weeks before the US invaded Venezuela to depose president Nicolas Maduro and launched air attacks on Iran.

Despite criticism, the Fifa ethics committee did not respond to complaints about Infantino's political neutrality over the prize.

At the start of the year, Infantino made a surprise appearance at the inaugural meeting of Trump's Board of Peace, set up to oversee the reconstruction of Gaza.

The International Olympic Committee, of which Infantino is an invited member, said its rules on political neutrality had not been breached.

However, many felt he had positioned himself too close to the US president.

This was heightened when USA striker Folarin Balogun escaped a ban after being sent off at the World Cup.

It was an unprecedented move by Fifa's disciplinary committee, with Trump saying he had personally called Infantino asking for the red card to be reviewed.

Infantino insisted it was a decision taken by an independent body over which no-one could have an influence.

On the final weekend of the World Cup, Trump and Infantino appeared together at Trump Tower in New York. The US president said he had called the Fifa president who "made another great decision".

Then, perhaps the culmination of Infantino's close association with Trump, came Fifa Forward Enterprise.

The private investor was to be a company linked to the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Uefa says boycott may still go ahead as FA withdraws Infantino support

Uefa boycott right thing for future of game - Bronze

If Infantino goes, who might replace him as Fifa president?

Independent questions of Infantino's methods and decisions are rare because he does not often speak to the media.

In the past four years he has given just two news conferences, both lasting an hour and held before the start of the World Cup.

Other than that, Infantino generally appears in Fifa-produced interviews issued through their official channels.

Before the 2026 World Cup, Infantino tried to head off at the pass any queries about high ticket prices and supporters' visas.

But, at the news conference before the World Cup, his reply of "just, you know, chill, relax" about Somali referee Omar Artan, who had been denied entry to the USA at Miami Airport, sparked concern.

The Fifa statement issued on Wednesday offered some contrition. But there was a rebuke, too.

It gave Infantino the chance to bite back, saying Fifa would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process".

The allure of the role is great, underscored by the fact there have been just four permanent Fifa presidents since Stanley Rous was elected in 1961.

Outside of Europe, the record revenues achieved by Infantino have funded the football operations of many countries. That has created loyalty, and it is a vote winner.

Yet for Uefa, and a few other national associations, the rap sheet is now too long.

Fifa cannot be run as an autocratic project any longer, claim his critics - many of them within European football.

Expanding the World Cup was in Infantino's election manifesto, and an increase to 64 teams for 2030 seems highly likely if he gets a fourth term.

There was also the expanded summer Club World Cup. The trophy is engraved with a personal tribute - "Inspired by the Fifa president Gianni Infantino".

The unique allocation of the next two men's World Cups helped ensure Saudi Arabia, another close ally of Infantino, would get the 2034 event.

The draw for this summer's World Cup was a long, lavish and outlandish affair. Trump was front and centre, as was Infantino.

Many supporters felt the price of tickets was too high, while some who were prepared to pay for them were denied visas.

Fifa opted to use a secondary market place with uncapped prices and a 30% share on each ticket sold.

Critics said profit had become more important than the supporter experience, with the attorneys general of New York and New Jersey subpoenaing Fifa to answer questions about its ticketing practices.

Even with all these controversies, Infantino was expected to be re-elected, such was his support around the world in many member associations.

Indeed, before the World Cup 111 had already declared for him - enough to guarantee re-election.

Now that picture is uncertain amid the fallout from Fifa's failed private investment plan.

Uefa sees this moment as its chance to force him to step down.

But, as his attendance at the Colombia president's inauguration shows, that may be incredibly difficult to achieve.

title: Miami Heat legend Udonis Haslem ‘proud to announce’ ownership stake in Premier League soccer club
description: Udonis Haslem is expanding his business portfolio with an investment in a newly promoted Premier League soccer club. The popularity of soccer has skyrocketed in the US following the conclusion of the 2026 FIFA World Cup.
fullText:
Udonis Haslem is expanding his business portfolio with an investment in a newly promoted Premier League soccer club.

The popularity of soccer has skyrocketed in the US following the conclusion of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The sport has gained a plethora of new fans.

This apparently includes Miami Heat legend and former NBA star Udonis Haslem, who has decided to pour in some of his hard-earned money into a newly promoted English Premier League club.

After playing for two decades in the NBA, Haslem has transitioned into an analyst role, primarily for Amazon Prime Video's coverage.

Haslem is now further branching out as the Heat legend announced his investment in newly promoted PL club, Ipswich Town on X.

"Basketball has been my life, but I've always respected the culture and impact of football. Proud to announce that last September, I became a minority owner of Ipswich Town Football Club.

"When I first saw the club's motto 'Running Towards Adversity,' I knew this was a club I wanted to be part of. Something I've believed in my entire career," Haslem wrote on X.

He added, "Then I met the people behind the club, and it became clear it was more than just words. It's who they are. That's the only kind of culture I want to be around.

"I'm excited to support what's being built at Ipswich…both on and off the pitch. Miami to Portman Road. NBA to the Premier League. Let's go, Blues!"

Haslem spent his entire career following the ever-so-famous Heat culture, and it feels like the NBA legend has found a club that perfectly embodies that sentiment.
